A former Arizona Senate president and chairman of the House Freedom Caucus, Biggs has built a national profile as one of Congress' most conservative lawmakers. Throughout his campaign, he emphasized border security, reducing government spending, opposing illegal immigration, expanding school choice, and rolling back regulations he argues have hurt Arizona businesses.
Hobbs secured her renomination without opposition, allowing her campaign to spend months preparing for the general election. Despite not facing a primary challenger, the governor invested millions of dollars in television advertising highlighting her administration's economic record and bipartisan work with Arizona's Republican-controlled Legislature while appealing to independent and moderate Republican voters.
"I've never lost an election, but I've also never won one alone. This will be a close race, but I'm excited to be in this fight with all of you to keep Arizona moving forward," Hobbs wrote on social media shortly after polls closed Tuesday evening.
Speaking to reporters before the primary, Hobbs said her campaign had already shifted its focus to the general election in November. "We are running the race we need to win, and it is going to take a lot to get there. We know it's going to be a close race," Hobbs said. "I'm proud of the support I've garnered and, you know, I'm not raising campaign money to haul it away. I'm raising it to spend."
Democrats view Arizona as a critical state for maintaining control of governorships in competitive battlegrounds, while Republicans see Biggs as a candidate capable of unifying the party and capitalizing on voter concerns over inflation, immigration, and the economy.

Arizona Republicans choose Rep. Andy Biggs to challenge Gov. Hobbs
PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Arizona Republicans on Tuesday selected their nominee to take on incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs in November, as the GOP seeks to regain a trifecta in the battleground state.
U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs won the nomination easily, according to unofficial results. The Associated Press called the race minutes after the results came in.
“Tonight’s results show that Arizonans overwhelmingly believe in our vision and I’m grateful to have earned their support,” Biggs said in a statement. “Our goal has always been to unite the Republican Party and we’ve done that as much as any nominee in recent memory.”
His closest competitor was fellow U.S. Rep. David Schweikert, who has served in Congress since 2011 and left his highly competitive swing-district seat open. Businessmen Scott Neely and Ken Miceli were also vying for the GOP nomination but are polling at 1%.
But while Trump’s endorsement is paramount in primaries, only one Republican since 2018, former Gov. Doug Ducey, has managed to win a statewide general election with Trump’s backing.
Hobbs was first elected to the governorship in 2022 by beating Trump-aligned candidate and former news anchor Kari Lake, who parroted a lot of the president’s election fraud theories, turned off McCain voters, and was viewed by some as too extreme.
Hobbs is seen as a vulnerable Democratic governor in a state President Donald Trump won in 2026 and who has thwarted much of Republicans’ agenda in the state Legislature with her veto pen.
Who is Andy Biggs?
Biggs built a national profile as chair of the House Freedom Caucus from 2019 to 2022 and as a staunch defender of Trump. He assisted the president’s attempt to block the certification of his loss in the 2020 election, voting against accepting Electoral College votes from Arizona and other battleground states after the Jan. 6 riot.
During the campaign Schweikert argued that Biggs is unelectable and would continue a decade of backsliding for Republicans in Arizona. The party has nominated a string of Trump loyalists who excited the GOP base but turned off independents and lost general elections, and Democrats now hold both of the state’s Senate seats and the top three state offices.
But Schweikert struggled to raise money and was unable to overcome Biggs’ advantages, including Trump’s endorsement and support from the Turning Point Action conservative group’s grassroots turnout machine.
Biggs said he can unite Republicans going into the general election.
“I am deeply honored to be chosen by Arizona Republicans as their nominee to defeat Katie Hobbs in November. This campaign has been driven by our grassroots supporters from the day we launched in January 2025 with a clear mission of Restoring the American Dream in our great state. Tonight’s results show that Arizonans overwhelmingly believe in our vision and I’m grateful to have earned their support. Our goal has always been to unite the Republican Party and we’ve done that as much as any nominee in recent memory.
As we advance to the General Election, I want to make sure every Arizonan knows this: no matter what your political party is or your background, you deserve a better leader than Katie Hobbs. I’m going to work day and night to earn your vote, finding the areas of agreement we have and making sure you know I’ll be a Governor for you and your family and your community.
Thank you again to everyone who volunteered, supported, donated, and voted for our campaign. Let’s go win in November!”
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Trump-backed Biggs, Feely, Lamb win GOP primaries in Arizona
sources.text:
Trump-backed Biggs, Feely, Lamb win GOP primaries in Arizona
Republicans backed by President Donald Trump won handily in Arizona, one of the nation's most competitive political battleground states, providing a pivotal snapshot heading into the 2026 midterm elections.
And so far, so good for GOP favorites as Rep. Andy Biggs, a 2020 election denier, secured the Republican nomination to face incumbent Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs in November. Hobbs was once considered the most vulnerable Democratic incumbent of this year's cycle, but experts believe it will be a difficult task for Biggs to court undecided independents, a key voting bloc in the state.
Meanwhile, President Trump-backed candidate and former NFL Pro Bowl kicker Jay Feely won the Republican primary in Arizona's key swing Congressional District 1. Alex Kolodin defeated Gina Swoboda to secure the GOP nomination for Secretary of State and will face incumbent Democrat Adrian Fontes in November.
And a third Trump-endorsed candidate, Mark Lamb, the scandal-scarred former sheriff of Pinal County, won the 5th Congressional District Republican primary over challenger Daniel Keenan. That primary squarely in the heart of MAGA country tested Trump's support of Lamb, who faced allegations of sexting, threats, intimidation, nude photo-sharing, and racist messages, undercutting his "America's Sheriff," TV image.
On the Democratic side, incumbent Rep. Greg Stanton beat progressive challenger and self-proclaimed democratic socialist Kai Newkirk, dashing the longshot hopes of a Mamdani-esque upset in the 4th Congressional District primary.
As a purple state in play, Arizona will play a critical role in who controls the House of Representatives next year. Trump won the state by about 6 percentage points two years ago, his best performance among the seven swing states.
Lamb surpasses scandals to win 5th Congressional GOP primary race
Laura Gersony and Terry Collins
Mark Lamb, the scandal-plagued former sheriff of Pinal County that was endorsed by President Donald Trump, overcame his obstacles to win the 5th Congressional District Republican primary, the Associated Press and NBC News projected.
Lamb was well ahead of his GOP rival, political newcomer Daniel Keenan, when the race was called late Tuesday.
The Arizona primary in the heart of MAGA country gauged the strength of Trump's endorsement, as Lamb faced allegations that undercut his image as a family-values candidate.
Lamb did little to push back as a months-long investigation by The Arizona Republic surfaced claims of sexting, threats, intimidation, nude photo-sharing, racist messages, and his recent purchase of a multimillion-dollar ranch property in Tennessee.
The allegations made waves in the conservative stronghold that has been represented by a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints for decades. Keenan spent his personal wealth on ads that put Lamb's allegations directly in front of voters.
However, a well-funded GOP group countered Keenan's attacks, buying television ads that reminded voters of Lamb's Trump endorsement.
Lamb's victory came as incumbent Rep. Andy Biggs vacated the seat to run for governor; Biggs won his primary race as well. Lamb will now face Democratic challenger Jennifer Lee, who also won her primary race on Tuesday.
Stanton cruises past progressive Newkirk in 4th congressional district
Terry Collins and Laura Gersony
Incumbent Democratic Rep. Greg Stanton has defeated progressive challenger and self-proclaimed democratic socialist Kai Newkirk, crushing left-wing dreams of a Mamdani-style upset in the 4th Congressional District primary, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ have projected.
With 76% of the vote in, Stanton, the centrist Democrat, had twice as many votes, 68%, compared to Newkirk's 31%. Newkirk, a community activist, struggled to build a base of support as he undertook a longshot effort to unseat the four-term incumbent.
Although Newkirk's campaign generated national attention among progressives, a series of lost endorsements also dimmed his once-promising campaign as his platform of opposing data centers drew pushback from big-money AI groups, who spent more than a quarter-million dollars on ads supporting Stanton.
And Newkirk had a mixed reception within the district ahead of the primary — even from the left-wing activist groups who embraced his political vision.
Stanton now faces Republican challenger Zudhi Jasser, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary ahead of November's general election.
Kolodin wins GOP Secretary of State nomination
Josh Meyer and James Powel
Alex Kolodin defeated Gina Swoboda to secure the GOP nomination for Secretary of State and will face incumbent Democrat Adrian Fontes in November, according to the Associated Press and NBC News.
Kolodin, a state representative from Scottsdale, is a lawyer who has garnered widespread attention for claiming that U.S. elections, including those in Arizona, are unfair and “rigged.”
He was part of the so-called “kraken” lawsuits involving Trump ally Sidney Powell that claimed “massive election fraud” in 2020. He also represented some of the Republican “fake electors” who hoped to set aside Arizona’s 2020 certified election results as part of Trump’s effort to overturn his election loss.
In the statehouse, the sophomore lawmaker has sponsored a state constitutional amendment that would allow counties to use hand-counted voting tallies, a method experts view as more error-prone than electronic counting.
The "Arizona Secure Elections Act" would also require voters to present government-issued identification to cast a ballot. Last month, the GOP-run legislature voted to place Kolodin’s plan on the fall general election ballot, avoiding a veto from Hobbs.
In Arizona, the secretary of state is primarily responsible for maintaining the statewide voter registration database, writing the state’s Elections Procedures Manual that translates elections statutes into a practical “how‑to” guide, and certifying election equipment.
Trump-endorsed Jay Feely wins GOP 1st Congressional District primary
Terry Collins
President Trump-backed candidate and former NFL Pro Bowl kicker Jay Feely has won the Republican primary in Arizona's key swing Congressional District 1, the Associated Press and NBC News have projected.
With nearly 69% of the vote in, Feely handily defeated former state Rep. Joe Chaplik and businessman John Trobough. Feely is seeking to replace retiring GOP Congressman and current Arizona gubernatorial candidate David Schweikert in the wealthy, metro-Phoenix-based congressional seat.
Feely initially ran for Congress for Arizona's 5th District, but switched to District 1 after Trump endorsed former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb, who became the clear front-runner.
But the 1st District could be a toss-up in November. Feely will either face Democratic primary challengers former state legislator Amish Shah and Marlene Galán-Woods, a former television news anchor endorsed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC).
The two Democrats squared off in the 2024 primary, with Shah beating Galán-Woods by about 1,700 votes. Shah eventually lost to Schweikert, but could be a contender again this year.
Biggs wins GOP governor primary, showdown with Hobbs set for November
Drew Pittock
Republican Rep. Andy Biggs clinched the GOP gubernatorial nomination, according to the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ.
While Biggs faced three challengers in tonight’s primary, his victory was all but sure. He was leading by as much as 50 percentage points in some surveys going into Election Day and he's been endorsed by Trump, a gold standard in most GOP primaries this year.
Now, Biggs will face off against incumbent Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs in November. Biggs' campaign said in a July 21 memo that it believes that Hobbs is "uniquely vulnerable" when it comes to her record, which includes a record 541 vetoes against proposals passed by the Republican-controlled legislature.
Biggs, 67, has served in Congress for nearly a decade and was the former chair of the arch-conservative House Freedom Caucus.
Shade rules cause controversy on triple-digit primary day
Ray Stern
On a day when Phoenix hit a high of 102 degrees, according to the Weather Channel, what could be wrong with shade tents at election sites?
Turns out, Arizona state law “does not allow the temporary or permanent construction of structures in public areas and parking lots.”
Poll workers were trained to let people at voting sites know they shouldn’t put up shade structures, said Jennifer Liewer, Maricopa County deputy elections director. However, the rule wasn’t being enforced July 21 because “it’s hot out” and it’s unclear if a pop-up tent is “structure,” Liewer said.
The law ruffled feathers at a few of the 236 polling sites in Maricopa County on July 21.
Facebook user Jeffrey Tucker complained in a post that the law was enforced only against a tent used by Democrats at a Chandler voting site. The tent ultimately wasn’t taken down.
Officials at two other sites called election headquarters about people who refused to take the tents down and were told a tent could stay up “as long as it’s not blocking a pathway,” Liewer said. “There will be further discussion about this” among election officials, she added.
When to expect the first results?
Taylor Seely
The first results are expected be released at around 11 p.m. ET/8 p.m. local time.
Arizona primary election results are unofficial until local and state officials have tallied all ballots and certified the results. The process can be slow, with mail-in ballots requiring signature verification and tabulation.
Those dropped off on Election Day likely won't all be counted until a couple of days later.
Arizona primary polls close
James Powel
Polls closed across Arizona at 10 p.m. ET/7 p.m. local time.
Results are set to start being released shortly.
Arizona voter worries about Dems like Zohran Mamdani
Stephanie Innes
Retiree Stana Kaigl voted in person during the afternoon heat at Emmanuel Presbyterian Church in north Phoenix.
The 85-year-old Republican moved to the U.S. from the Czech Republic in 1969. She said the best outcome for the primary and the general would be if the Democrats don't do well and that she worries about Democrats like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
"What he's doing, it won't work," she said.
Progressive candidate hoping to pull a Mamdani-esque upset
Terry Collins and Laura Gersony
A Democratic face-off in Arizona's 4th Congressional District is pitting progressive newcomer and self-proclaimed democratic socialist Kai Newkirk against a well-established centrist incumbent, Rep. Greg Stanton.
Despite garnering national attention among progressives who thought Newkirk might have a chance of winning amid a national anti-establishment surge that occurred with democratic socialist candidates in New York (backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani) and Colorado, the community organizer might be a flash in the pan against the four-term Stanton.
That's because Newkirk has struggled to win support from within the district, even from the left-wing activist groups who initially embraced his vision.
A series of lost endorsements has also dimmed Newkirk's once-promising campaign as he wanted his race to be a referendum on Israel, resistance to Trump, and other issues that have fueled left-wing candidates to upset wins.
"A late entry into the race, significantly less fundraising than Stanton, and no labor backing has put Newkirk at a strategic disadvantage, and put the District in the position of risking a fascist ghoul taking the seat in the fall," the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America wrote in their 2026 candidate guide.
"After long and careful consideration as a committee, we are offering no recommendation in this race," the DSA concluded.
Also, Stanton is a staunch moderate, serving in a leadership role for the party's centrist New Democrats bloc in the U.S. House. A former Phoenix mayor, Stanton has been reelected to Congress every two years since 2018.
Arizona voter wants to do away with politicians
Robert Anglen
Retired Navy veteran Allen Eckert, 85, said he came to vote in person at Walker Butte Middle School in San Tan Valley because it’s his civic duty. He was alone outside the polling station in Pinal County.
“I feel most people don’t do it anymore. They don’t think it matters,” he said. “If we did away with politicians, we’d have a better world.”
Eckert said he wants to make Andy Biggs Arizona’s governor because the Republican can better handle the economy. He said rising costs are a key concern.
He was less convinced about Mark Lamb replacing Biggs in Congress, referencing a series of sex scandals that have plagued the former Pinal County Sheriff.
“I don’t know if everything they are saying about him is true, but I’m leaning somewhere else,” Eckert said.
Election experts weigh in on the DOJ's decision to monitor primaries
Drew Pittock
After the Justice Department said it was sending election "monitors" to several key counties in Arizona for today’s primaries, several election experts weighed in on the decision.
Bill Gates, executive director of Arizona State University's Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory, was a former Republican election day operations attorney and Maricopa County Supervisor. He said that DOJ election monitors are “nothing new.”
"Their presence has been a routine part of elections under administrations of both parties and has been intended to help ensure compliance with federal voting rights laws,” Gates said.
Meanwhile, Dr. Christopher Weber, director of the Voter Project at the University of Arizona, described the DOJ's decision to send election monitors into a state during an active primary as "highly unusual."
Weber, who votes in Pima County, said his experience at the polls today "was no different from any other."
"The county recorders and poll workers I've interacted with follow the same procedures every cycle, including verifying registrations and issuing ballots," Weber said. "This matches what I observe in my academic research: I regularly work with the state's voter file, a large but incredibly transparent set of records, which anyone can request from the Secretary of State's office."
Arizona voters express election concerns
Erick Trevino and Stephanie Innes
Voters casting their ballot on Election Day said recent events raised questions about election integrity for them.
Devin Deupree, 22, who lives in Phoenix and voted at the ASU A.E. England Building in downtown Phoenix, said he thinks the country is in a political crisis with President Trump using the 2020 election as an excuse to say ballots and elections are not trustworthy.
“I think that’s just a way for him to implement some sort of voter registration to track who’s voting for what, believing in what, and then that’s going to infringe more on our freedoms,” he said.
Brenna Tonelli, 40, of Chandler, decided to vote close to her work offices in downtown Phoenix and said she was inclined to drop off her ballot in person over concerns that her mail-in ballot will not get counted.
“I wasn’t going to mail it in because I’m worried about what will happen when it leaves my hands,” she said.
Tyler Zaino cast an in-person ballot at 9:30 a.m. at Shadow Rock Congregational United Church of Christ in the north of Phoenix to ensure his vote will get counted properly, he said.
Once an Obama Democrat, Zaino now describes himself as a "pretty staunch Republican" and plans to vote in person for the general election.
The father of two who works as a security guard used to always vote by mail due to his busy schedule but said he’s recently lost “significant confidence” in the mail-in process.
NJ software vendor has ties to Arizona
Stephanie Murray
The software vendor at the center of a New Jersey voter registration controversy provided driver’s licenses and state IDs in Arizona.
New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill said that a software error led to 6,600 people being registered to vote from 2023-2024, although they indicated they were not citizens. Some 400 noncitizens voted as a result, according to Sherrill. The vendor is Idemia.
No immediate connections were found to Arizona’s voter registration system.
“ADOT MVD does not use the same vendor as New Jersey did,” Arizona Department of Transportation spokesperson Bill Lamoreaux said.
However, Idemia supplied physical IDs for Arizona from 2015 to 2023, records show. Most recently, Idemia launched mobile driver’s licenses and state IDs for Samsung Wallet with the ADOT Motor Vehicle Division from 2023 to 2025.
The Arizona Secretary of State’s office declined to comment and directed inquiries to ADOT.
Viewpoints clash at Phoenix community college as voters head to polls
Stephanie Innes
Alex Jacome shook his head as he came out of the polling station at Paradise Valley Community College shortly after 11 a.m local time. The 66-year-old was not pleased with the two Republican tents just outside the 75-foot electioneering area.
Jacome, who is a registered Independent, was Republican until Donald Trump got into office, he said.
“Republicans need to be removed from office everywhere,” he said. “I take my voting responsibility seriously.”
Turning Point Action were among the conservative tents just outside the 75-foot electioneering barrier set up at the community college located in the north of Phoenix. Turning Point Action is the political arm of the right-wing Turning Point USA founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
Turning Point Action Committee employee Clarissa Cosgrove’s red tent drew a small crowd of voters picking up stickers, flags, pamphlets and a list of the conservative organization’s choices for the primary, including Andy Biggs for governor, Alexander Kolodin for Secretary of State and Kimberly Yee for Superintendent of Public Instruction.
“We are sharing the love of voting,” Cosgrove said. “We want people to be proud of being Americans. We are the greatest country in the world.”
Twenty-three-year-old Nikita Joyner also voted at the community college. She said she knows people who don’t vote because they don’t think their vote matters but the physical therapy tech and dancer takes the opposite view.
“It’s so important,” Joyner said. “I’m really upset about how the country is currently being run. The most peaceful way to approach that is voting. … I think everyone needs to be out there voting.”
Secretary of state releases snapshot of early voting numbers
Drew Pittock
Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes’ office released preliminary early voting numbers for Tuesday’s primaries. Early voting kicked off June 24.
According to Fontes’ office, 852,369 ballots were returned statewide as of July 20.
The Grand Canyon State was also able to increase registration for its mail ballot tracking system by 73%, according to the secretary of state’s office. Arizona uses BallotTrax to help its rural communities stay engaged with the voting process by providing text or email updates as a ballot makes its way through the mail.
Without providing an exact number, the secretary’s office noted that voter turnout is shaping up to be pretty strong, as compared to previous cycles.
"I want to send a special thanks to our poll workers today," Fontes said. "Ensuring every Arizona voter has a safe and secure voting process is paramount and no one works harder than those on the ground in our counties. I am extremely proud of the work my office has done to support our election officials across the state and I look forward to a great Election Day."
GOP voters will decide Tuesday who should challenge Fontes for his office in November. The role has gained outsized influence in recent years, after President Donald Trump lost the state in 2020 and accused its elections of being rigged against him.
Will Hobbs debate Biggs?
Phillip M. Bailey
One lingering subject line in the 2026 Arizona gubernatorial race will be if Hobbs participates in a one-on-one debate this fall.
During the last campaign she refused to joust with Kari Lake, claiming the former TV news anchor would break decorum rules with "constant interruptions, pointless distractions, and childish name-calling." The Hobbs campaign cited how her GOP opponent at the time was a "conspiracy theorist" who spread Trump's false claims about 2020 election.
Biggs has similarly been at the center of denying that election's outcome, but he has avoided some of the other MAGA-aligned grievances – e.g. COVID-19 conspiracies – and has a different style, making it harder to label him as Lake's ideological twin.
The last televised debate Hobbs participated in was October 2018, according to Arizona TV stations, when she ran for secretary of state. At the moment she continues to defend the stiff arm tactic, saying she's given out plenty of information for voters to make their decision which suggests she won't be doing one this fall either.
The congressman's campaign, meanwhile, is already planting seed that she is "unable to defend her record in public or on the debate stage."
"Winning campaigns are led by candidates that show up to events, are willing to debate, and can make their case to voters through a variety of local and national media outlets," a Biggs campaign memo said.
5th District GOP primary to test scandals, strength of Trump endorsement
Terry Collins and Laura Gersony
A major question in Arizona's congressional primaries is whether Trump-backed former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb can overcome allegations of making threats, sexting, and sharing racist and homophobic texts to defeat Republican challenger Daniel Keenan in conservative-leaning District 5.
The primary winner will replace GOP Rep. Andy Biggs, who is vacating the seat to run for Arizona governor.
Lamb did little to push back as a months-long investigation by The Arizona Republic, part of the USA TODAY Network, surfaced claims of sexting, threats, intimidation, nude photo-sharing, sending racist messages and his recent purchase of a multimillion-dollar ranch property in Tennessee.
The allegations raised eyebrows in the district that has been represented by a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints for decades. It even led Lamb's underdog opponent, construction business owner Keenan, to spend his personal wealth on ads putting the allegations squarely before voters.
Keenan has fashioned himself as a scandal-free alternative to Lamb and emphasized that he, too, was in lockstep with Trump. Lamb, a charismatic personality and a regular speaker at Trump's rallies for years, has curated an image as "America's Sheriff" by frequently appearing on cable news and reality television shows, gaining a large online following in the process.
But Lamb could be ripe for an upset, Thom Reilly, a professor and co-director of the Center for an Independent and Sustainable Democracy at Arizona State University, told USA TODAY.
"Keenan could pull it off, you never know," Reilly said. "But Lamb, with that Trump stamp of approval, that might just be enough for him to prevail in the primary."
Why Hobbs is considered vulnerable
Phillip M. Bailey
From the start of this campaign Gov. Katie Hobbs has been called the "most vulnerable" Democratic incumbent of the 2026 cycle even amid a projected "blue wave" for her party this fall.
That moniker is based largely on Arizona's swing stage status, which begins with Hobbs' razor-thing victory in 2022 over Republican Kari Lake, a MAGA-coded loyalist, by less than one percentage point. Two years later Trump won the Grand Canyon state by about six percentage points, which was his best performance among the seven swing states that he swept.
Biggs' campaign said in a July 21 memo that it believes that Hobbs is "uniquely vulnerable" when it comes to her record, which includes a record 541 vetoes against proposals passed by the Republican-controlled legislature.
Arizona is also among the least affordable with household costs that have increased faster than national rates. Since 2019, for instance, the state's households have had to spend about $19,300 more on essential expenses per year compared with the national average of roughly $15,400.
At a time when affordability is putting most Republicans on their heels Biggs has been aggressive about making that an advantage. He is proposing to eliminate the state income tax to help out average Arizonans, for instance.
"I know this race is going to be close no matter what because Arizona is a swing state," Hobbs told USA TODAY in a email statement. "I'm going to earn every vote by showing Arizonans how I'm putting what’s best for the state ahead of partisan politics – lowering costs, securing the border, and bringing good-paying jobs here – and that's how I’ll win this race."
When do polls close?
Sarah D. Wire
Arizona is the only state holding a primary July 21. Polling locations there are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time on Election Day.
Find polling locations at the Secretary of State's website.
Can Trump-endorsed Jay Feely kick his way to a primary win?
Terry Collins
In Arizona's key swing Congressional District 1, former NFL Pro Bowl kicker Jay Feely is seeking to capitalize on his name recognition and President Donald Trump's endorsement to defeat former state Rep. Joe Chaplik and businessman John Trobough.
The three candidates are vying to replace retiring Republican congressman and current Arizona gubernatorial candidate David Schweikert in this wealthy, metro-Phoenix-based congressional seat.
The three candidates don't vary much on policy, as they support Trump's agenda on top issues like immigration, economic policy, and the war with Iran. But the race has become contentious over the use of artificial intelligence, dividing the district's loyal GOP base.
Feely favors the technology, arguing that AI data centers can benefit local communities and emphasizing their importance to national security. Chaplik is more skeptical, saying he would oppose any data centers in the district that his constituents didn't want. Trobough, a former cybersecurity company CEO, has emphasized that his experience will better position Arizona on AI and other tech issues.
But getting the support from Trump could be what puts Feely over the top, said Thom Reilly, a professor and codirector of the Center for an Independent and Sustainable Democracy at Arizona State University. Feely initially ran for Congress for the 5th District, but switched districts after Trump endorsed former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb, who became the clear front-runner.
"Given how Trump endorsements have basically worked everywhere else, I can't see why it wouldn't work this time here," Reilly said about Feely's chances of winning the open seat in District 1.
Most important race could be down ballot
Josh Meyer
The most consequential election in Arizona this year may not be for governor or Congress, but for a statewide office that rarely makes national headlines but helps administer the races that do.
Republicans are set to decide who will take on incumbent Democrat Adrian Fontes to be Arizona’s secretary of state in November.
Alex Kolodin has a wide lead over Gina Swoboda in the race, according to a recent NextGen Polling poll.
Kolodin, a state representative from Scottsdale, is a lawyer who has garnered widespread attention for claiming that U.S. elections, including those in Arizona, are unfair and “rigged.” Swoboda worked in the secretary of state’s office under a Republican and a Democrat and headed the state Republican Party with Trump’s blessing.
In Arizona, the secretary of state is primarily responsible for maintaining the statewide voter registration database, writing the state’s Elections Procedures Manual that translates elections statutes into a practical “how‑to” guide, and certifying election equipment.
But the job has become a “bully pulpit” of sorts since 2020, when then-Secretary of State Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, used it to push back on claims by Trump and his Arizona supporters that the election in the state was rigged against him, said former elected Maricopa County Recorder Stephen Richer.
“I think the secretary does have a powerful role now, in terms of being the ostensible chief spokesperson for election administration,” Richer, a Republican who now analyzes election administration and democracy as a senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School, told USA TODAY.
Biggs uses primary for political makeover
Phillip M. Bailey
Republican Rep. Andy Biggs is expecting to win in the July 21 gubernatorial primary by a wide margin against his three rivals, according to a campaign memo.
He's leading by as much as 50 percentage points in some surveys and he's been endorsed by Trump, which has proven to be the gold standard in most GOP primaries this year.
That has given the 67-year-old former chair of the House Freedom Caucus a chance to reintroduce himself to Arizona voters, specifically by showcasing his occasional bipartisan efforts in Washington.
Among the measures Biggs cites is a 2018 proposal he co-sponsored with Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, now the Democrats' minority leader, to require more reporting from lobbyists.
"I may be conservative, but I've also shown that even when you're conservative, if you look to collaborate, you can find points and ways to collaborate with even people who fundamentally disagree with you on other things," Biggs told USA TODAY in a one-on-one interview July 17.
Who is running for Arizona governor?
James Powel
Tuesday's primaries will set the field for November's gubernatorial election.
Incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs is running unopposed in the Democratic primary.
Rep. Andy Biggs is the presumptive favorite to win the Republican nomination to challenge her in the fall but faces fellow Rep. David Schweikert; Ken Miceli, who owns a company that specializes in repainting homes; and Scott Neely, who sells concrete supplies.
House races to watch
Sarah D. Wire
Arizona's congressional primary races may determine whether Republicans can maintain their slight edge in the U.S. House. Six of the state's nine U.S. House seats are held by Republicans.
In District 1's Republican primary, former NFL player Jay Feely aims to capitalize on Trump's backing to replace David Schweikert, a retiring GOP congressman running for Arizona governor. Feely has to hold off former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik and and businessman John Trobough to gain the nomination.
In that district, Democrats will choose between former state legislator Amish Shah and Marlene Galán-Woods, a former television news anchor endorsed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC). The primary is a rematch of 2024 when Shah won the nomination and went on the lose to Schweikert in 2024.
Another Trump-endorsed choice, former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb, is hoping he can overcome allegations of sexting and sharing racist and homophobic texts to defeat Republican challenger Daniel Keenan in the conservative-leaning 5th Congressional District. Keenan has spent $1.65 million to run an ad that describes Lamb as an unfit candidate.
Democrats running for the 5th District nomination are Brian Hualde, Chris James and Elizabeth Lee. The district has been held by Republicans for the past 15 years.
And a Democratic face-off in the 4th Congressional District pits progressive newcomer Kai Newkirk, a community organizer, against a well-established centrist incumbent, Rep. Greg Stanton.
Stanton holds a leadership role for the party's centrist New Democrats bloc in the U.S. House. He was first elected in 2018.
Justice Department sends election monitors to Maricopa, Apache and Pima counties
Josh Meyer
The Justice Department is sending election "monitors" to several key counties in Arizona today to watch for election fraud and other problems, according to Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon.
In an X post, Dhillon said "election monitors are fanning out in Maricopa, Apache, and Pima counties for the Arizona primary today."
"ALL citizens and ONLY citizens should get out and vote in federal races today, feeling confident that the government is here to help!" Dhillon wrote.
What are Arizona's politics?
Sarah D. Wire
Arizona has traditionally been a heavily Republican state, and six of its nine House members are Republican.
But the state currently has a Democratic governor, and both U.S. senators are Democrats. The state voted for former President Joe Biden in 2020, but flipped back in 2024 for President Donald Trump.
As of July, 1.5 million – or 35.39% of registered voters – were Republican, according to the Secretary of State's office.
Another 1.49 million – or 34.6% of registered voters – were independents. And 1.3 million – or 28.11% of registered voters – were Democrats.
The high number of independent voters has made Arizona a true battleground and an expected heavy target in the 2028 presidential race.

PHOENIX - The Associated Press is projecting that incumbent Democrat Katie Hobbs and GOP's Andy Biggs will advance to the general election in November.

Biggs, who is currently a Congressman, ran in a GOP primary that featured three other candidates: Ken Miceli, Scott Neely, and David Schweikert.
Meanwhile, Democrat Katie Hobbs ran unopposed in her party's gubernatorial primary.
What they're saying:
In a post made to Facebook, Gov. Hobbs said she is "grateful to every Arizonan who’s already shown up for this campaign."
"This will be a close race, but I’m excited to be in this fight with all of you to keep Arizona moving forward," read a portion of her post.
In a statement posted on X with the caption "Let's go WIN in November, Arizona!", Biggs said he is "deeply honored to be chosen by Arizona Republicans as their nominee to defeat Katie Hobbs in November."
"No matter what your political party is or your background, you deserve a better leader than Katie Hobbs," read a portion of the statement.
Biggs addressed his supporters late Tuesday night.
"I love this state. I know you do too. Let's make this the year we turn Arizona red again and build the red wall, and we set the stage for 2028 as well. Thank you for being here. The real work begins tomorrow. I'll be working my tail off, and you will too. It's too important.
The backstory:
According to the Associated Press, Biggs built a national profile as chair of the House Freedom Caucus from 2019 to 2022, and as a staunch defender of President Donald Trump.
The AP states that during the campaign, GOP gubernatorial candidate Schweikert argued that Biggs is unelectable. Schweikert, however, struggled to raise money and was not able to overcome Biggs' advantages, which included an endorsement from Trump.
The other side:
Hobbs' campaign has wasted no time in attacking Biggs. In an email sent on the night of July 21, her campaign announced the release of a new video that attacked Biggs' record in Congress.
Officials with Hobbs' campaign say the video "details Biggs' record of siding with billionaires over working families."

PHOENIX — U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, a fierce ally of President Donald Trump and former head of the House Freedom Caucus, won the Republican nomination for Arizona governor Tuesday.
Biggs took the stage late Tuesday night to speak after his projected win for the GOP governor's primary. Watch in the player below:
Click here to see the live results as they come in
Democrats were locked in a close primary contest for a battleground U.S. House district, with emergency physician Amish Shah leading party-backed Marlene Galán-Woods for the chance to take on Jay Feely, the former Arizona Cardinals kicker who won the Republican nomination with Trump's endorsement.
A Shah victory would be another defeat for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which has occasionally struggled this year as voters seek out antiestablishment candidates. The race was too early to call early Wednesday morning.
Biggs overwhelmingly defeated fellow U.S. Rep. David Schweikert in the primary and will face Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs in what could be one of the closest governor races in November.
By choosing Biggs, who supported Trump's failed attempt to block certification of his 2020 election loss, Republican voters risk nominating another conservative warrior who excites the party base but fails to win a general election by turning off independents. Although the party once dominated Arizona, Democrats now hold both U.S. Senate seats and the top three state offices.
Biggs faced travel problems leaving a Republican Governors Association meeting in Colorado, according to senior adviser Drew Sexton, and didn’t reach his victory party in Scottsdale until more than three hours after he won the race. By the time he took the stage, the crowd of hundreds had dwindled to dozens and he spoke to a mostly empty room.
“Let’s make this the year that we turn Arizona red again,” Biggs said.
Schweikert argued during the campaign that Biggs would continue a decade of Republican backsliding. However, he struggled to raise money and did not even return to Arizona for Election Day, remaining in Washington as the House passed a government funding bill.
Biggs rejected Schweikert's claim that he'll be another Republican judged by voters to be too extreme.
“I am a conservative — and a principled conservative — but I work with people that don’t necessarily agree with me on every issue,” Biggs told a reporter after his victory speech.
Biggs, who had Trump's endorsement and support from the grassroots organization Turning Point Action, said he can unite Republicans going into the general election.
“Everyone I have talked to is really conservative around here,” said Ray Roberts, a 33-year-old Republican who works as a processing engineer and knocked on doors for Biggs. “We all have mostly conservative values. I think Arizona is a red state. I think Andy will be the winner in November.”
State Rep. Alexander Kolodin won the Republican nomination to challenge Democratic Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, defeating Gina Swoboda, the former Arizona Republican Party chair. Kolodin, a lawyer, was sanctioned by the state bar over his involvement with two 2020 election cases that courts found baseless, including one alleging the vote was marred by fraud and demanding Biden's victory in the state be overturned.
State Senate President Warren Petersen won the Republican nomination for attorney general and will face Democratic incumbent Kris Mayes, who won four years ago by just 280 votes out of more than 2.5 million.
Biggs and Schweikert responded differently to Trump's GOP takeover
Biggs built a national profile as chair of the House Freedom Caucus from 2019 to 2022 and as a staunch defender of Trump. He assisted the president’s attempt to block the certification of his loss in the 2020 election, voting against accepting Electoral College votes from Arizona and other battleground states after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot.
He has always represented safe Republican seats and is a veteran of factional brawls within his party. Before going to Congress, he nearly lost his post as state Senate president during a confrontation with then-Gov. Jan Brewer, also a Republican, over her push to expand Medicaid.
“I want the border secured. I want the police and more money spent in the right places like education,” said Kate Rouleau, a 67-year-old Republican who voted for Biggs because he "has the same quality as President Trump.”
Democrats focused their attacks on Biggs, whom they plan to portray as an extremist focused on helping Trump and not Arizonans.
In a statement Tuesday night, Hobbs said that “the more Arizonans learn about Biggs, the more they’ll realize he’s one big problem they can’t afford.”
The race is likely to be another close contest four years after Hobbs narrowly beat Republican firebrand Kari Lake by less than 1 percentage point. Republicans have since expanded their advantage in the state, growing GOP registration by 6% while Democratic registration fell by 4%.
Repeating her victory will require Hobbs to again win a majority of independents and some disaffected Republicans. For his part, Biggs has attacked her as a weak leader who presided over rising costs.
"We can’t let the state go to somebody who's actually recklessly incompetent, and that is our current governor," he said.
Primaries set the field for a top House battleground
Both parties had hotly contested primaries to replace Schweikert in the highly competitive 1st Congressional District, which both parties are targeting in the fight to control the House.
Feely won the Republican primary over Joseph Chaplik, a former state legislator popular with many grassroots activists, and businessperson John Trobough. Feely had Trump’s endorsement but has been dogged by criticism for living outside the district.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee threw its support behind Galán-Woods, a controversial decision to get involved in a contested primary that rankled some party activists. Her late husband, Grant Woods, was the Republican attorney general in the 1990s and later became a vocal Trump critic.
Galán-Woods’ chief opponent, Shah, is a former state legislator who was the nominee in 2024 but lost narrowly to Schweikert.
“We have a long tradition in Arizona of being independent-minded and working for the benefit of people,” Shah said at his election night party in Phoenix. “I wasn’t exactly my party’s pick. And I was willing to stand up to that establishment. And that’s what the voters of this district want.”
If Shah's lead holds, he would be the third Democrat to beat a DCCC-backed rival this year following Randy Villegas in California and Matt Dunlap in Maine. Unlike the candidates in those races, Shah and Galán-Woods are largely aligned ideologically.
Linda Bandler, a 65-year-old independent who volunteered on the Galán-Woods campaign, said the party will be in good shape regardless of who wins the primary.
“There still is some sanity,” said Bandler, who, like Galán-Woods, is a former Republican. “I do think that the Democrats will take over the House and the Senate.”
DCCC support generally brings an influx of money and staffing, both from the party itself and from the donors and interest groups that take its cues. But this election season, substantial parts of the Democratic base are rejecting candidates that party bosses see as their best shot at winning in Congress.
“The Democratic Party needs to grow up and wake up,” said Maria Liong, a 24-year-old medical student who volunteered for Shah’s campaign. “They need to realize that they want candidates who listen to their people.”
Republicans hold a voter registration advantage in the affluent district, which includes northeast Phoenix, Scottsdale, Fountain Hills and Paradise Valley.
But it started to trend toward the center after Trump’s 2016 victory. Redistricting accelerated the trend, fueling Democratic hopes that the seat could be flipped.
In Tucson, retired Marine drill instructor JoAnna Mendoza ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination to challenge second-term Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani, who also had no primary opponent. The seat is perennially competitive in general elections and is a top pickup target for Democrats in November.
Meanwhile, Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb won the Republican primary for the conservative district that Biggs is vacating. The race turned salacious as Lamb, who was endorsed by Trump, came under scrutiny for alleged sexual misconduct and abuse of power.
The county attorney cleared him of criminal wrongdoing, and Trump reiterated his endorsement this month. Lamb dismissed the allegations as “slander and lies.”

Schweikert argued during the campaign that Biggs would continue a decade of Republican backsliding. However, he struggled to raise money and did not even return to Arizona for Election Day, remaining in Washington as the House passed a government funding bill.
Biggs rejected Schweikert’s claim that he’ll be another Republican judged by voters to be too extreme.
“I am a conservative — and a principled conservative — but I work with people that don’t necessarily agree with me on every issue,” Biggs told a reporter after his victory speech.
Biggs, who had Trump’s endorsement and support from the grassroots organization Turning Point Action, said he can unite Republicans going into the general election.
“Everyone I have talked to is really conservative around here,” said Ray Roberts, a 33-year-old Republican who works as a processing engineer and knocked on doors for Biggs. “We all have mostly conservative values. I think Arizona is a red state. I think Andy will be the winner in November.”
State Rep. Alexander Kolodin won the Republican nomination to challenge Democratic Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, defeating Gina Swoboda, the former Arizona Republican Party chair. Kolodin, a lawyer, was sanctioned by the state bar over his involvement with two 2020 election cases that courts found baseless, including one alleging the vote was marred by fraud and demanding Biden’s victory in the state be overturned.
State Senate President Warren Petersen won the Republican nomination for attorney general and will face Democratic incumbent Kris Mayes, who won four years ago by just 280 votes out of more than 2.5 million.
Biggs and Schweikert responded differently to Trump’s GOP takeover
Biggs built a national profile as chair of the House Freedom Caucus from 2019 to 2022 and as a staunch defender of Trump. He assisted the president’s attempt to block the certification of his loss in the 2020 election, voting against accepting Electoral College votes from Arizona and other battleground states after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot.
He has always represented safe Republican seats and is a veteran of factional brawls within his party. Before going to Congress, he nearly lost his post as state Senate president during a confrontation with then-Gov. Jan Brewer, also a Republican, over her push to expand Medicaid.
“I want the border secured. I want the police and more money spent in the right places like education,” said Kate Rouleau, a 67-year-old Republican who voted for Biggs because he “has the same quality as President Trump.”
Democrats focused their attacks on Biggs, whom they plan to portray as an extremist focused on helping Trump and not Arizonans.
In a statement Tuesday night, Hobbs said that “the more Arizonans learn about Biggs, the more they’ll realize he’s one big problem they can’t afford.”
The race is likely to be another close contest four years after Hobbs narrowly beat Republican firebrand Kari Lake by less than 1 percentage point. Republicans have since expanded their advantage in the state, growing GOP registration by 6% while Democratic registration fell by 4%.
Repeating her victory will require Hobbs to again win a majority of independents and some disaffected Republicans. For his part, Biggs has attacked her as a weak leader who presided over rising costs.
“We can’t let the state go to somebody who’s actually recklessly incompetent, and that is our current governor,” he said.
Primaries set the field for a top House battleground
Both parties had hotly contested primaries to replace Schweikert in the highly competitive 1st Congressional District, which both parties are targeting in the fight to control the House.
Feely won the Republican primary over Joseph Chaplik, a former state legislator popular with many grassroots activists, and businessperson John Trobough. Feely had Trump’s endorsement but has been dogged by criticism for living outside the district.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee threw its support behind Galán-Woods, a controversial decision to get involved in a contested primary that rankled some party activists. Her late husband, Grant Woods, was the Republican attorney general in the 1990s and later became a vocal Trump critic.
Galán-Woods’ chief opponent, Shah, is a former state legislator who was the nominee in 2024 but lost narrowly to Schweikert.
“We have a long tradition in Arizona of being independent-minded and working for the benefit of people,” Shah said at his election night party in Phoenix. “I wasn’t exactly my party’s pick. And I was willing to stand up to that establishment. And that’s what the voters of this district want.”
If Shah’s lead holds, he would be the third Democrat to beat a DCCC-backed rival this year following Randy Villegas in California and Matt Dunlap in Maine. Unlike the candidates in those races, Shah and Galán-Woods are largely aligned ideologically.
Linda Bandler, a 65-year-old independent who volunteered on the Galán-Woods campaign, said the party will be in good shape regardless of who wins the primary.
“There still is some sanity,” said Bandler, who like Galán-Woods is a former Republican. “I do think that the Democrats will take over the House and the Senate.”
DCCC support generally brings an influx of money and staffing, both from the party itself and from the donors and interest groups that take its cues. But this election season, substantial parts of the Democratic base are rejecting candidates that party bosses see as their best shot at winning in Congress.
“The Democratic Party needs to grow up and wake up,” said Maria Liong, a 24-year-old medical student who volunteered for Shah’s campaign. “They need to realize that they want candidates who listen to their people.”
Republicans hold a voter registration advantage in the affluent district, which includes northeast Phoenix, Scottsdale, Fountain Hills and Paradise Valley.
But it started to trend toward the center after Trump’s 2016 victory. Redistricting accelerated the trend, fueling Democratic hopes that the seat could be flipped.
In Tucson, retired Marine drill instructor JoAnna Mendoza ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination to challenge second-term Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani, who also had no primary opponent. The seat is perennially competitive in general elections and is a top pickup target for Democrats in November.
Meanwhile, Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb won the Republican primary for the conservative district that Biggs is vacating. The race turned salacious as Lamb, who was endorsed by Trump, came under scrutiny for alleged sexual misconduct and abuse of power.
The county attorney cleared him of criminal wrongdoing, and Trump reiterated his endorsement this month. Lamb dismissed the allegations as “slander and lies.”

Associated Press writer Josh Kelety contributed.

SERGIO ARELLANO: The Bullish Case For Biggs
sources.text:
By Sergio Arellano |
The prediction markets say Katie Hobbs is a heavy favorite. The pundits agree. I’ve heard long odds before — I heard them in combat, and I heard them in January when I ran for Party Chair. Here’s what the gamblers and pundits are missing.
This election comes down to one thing: who shows up. And I like our side of that math.
Republicans are the largest voting bloc in Arizona — 1.54 million strong, per the Secretary of State, a 321,000-voter lead over the Democrats. That lead has grown by more than 170,000 voters since 2022: we’ve added nearly 110,000 registrants while Democrats have lost more than 60,000. Their own DNC chair admits Democrats have “been getting our butts kicked” on registration — his words — shedding 2.1 million voters nationwide from 2020 to 2024. He’s right.
Republicans are the most reliable midterm voters in this state — we show up, every cycle, like clockwork. Independents don’t, not in midterms, and 2026 has no presidential race and no Senate race. Governor is the top of the ballot. Hobbs’s entire polling lead is parked with the voters least likely to vote. Ours is built on the voters most likely to show. Monster Republican turnout, uninspiring veto queen, low-turnout independent voters — and her lead evaporates.
And this time, no one has to guess whether their vote counts. The days of Republicans sitting home because they don’t trust the process are over. The RNC and AZGOP already have boots on the ground — Arizona is a priority state in the RNC’s multimillion-dollar election integrity operation, with a state director in place and thousands of trained poll workers, poll watchers, and observers being recruited right now. Eyes and ears on every vote cast and every vote counted. And because we’ve learned the Left doesn’t just campaign — they litigate — our attorneys are on offense: the RNC’s legal team is waging more than 130 election integrity lawsuits across the country, including here at home, where we’ve gone to court to defend Arizona’s early-ballot list maintenance laws and hold Secretary Fontes accountable. Leftist lawfare doesn’t get a free shot at this election. Not on my watch.
Trust the process, bank your ballot early, bring your neighbor. That’s the whole playbook.
Meanwhile, look at the incumbent. Hobbs’s disapproval has climbed to 43% and rising. Most Arizonans have never once said the state is on the right track under her. She squeaked by in 2022 by 17,117 votes. And she’ll spend this fall dodging questions about four separate pay-to-play inquiries — including a criminal probe by her own Party’s attorney general, whose investigators have asked to interview her as they close out a two-year investigation. Hobbs is uncomfortable talking about it. She’s nervous. She vetoed transparency legislation. Twice. Arizonans notice.
Andy Biggs doesn’t have her problems. He has a united party standing fully behind its nominee, the biggest voter bloc in Arizona, and a turnout machine that’s already running.
The gambling markets say Katie Hobbs. I’m the chairman of 1.5 million people who’d like to say otherwise. A lot of people are about to learn that they shouldn’t gamble against Arizona voters.
Sergio Arellano serves as Chairman of the Arizona Republican Party.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – The Republican Governors Association (RGA) released the following statement in response to the Arizona Republican gubernatorial primary:
“Congratulations to Andy Biggs on his primary victory. Throughout his career in public service, Andy has fought to lower costs, grow Arizona’s economy, unleash American energy, and secure the border,” said RGA Chair Governor Greg Gianforte. “As governor, Andy will continue to put Arizona families first while Katie Hobbs focuses on serving special interests instead of addressing affordability, increasing the supply of housing, and creating more good-paying jobs. Arizonans have a clear choice this November, and Andy Biggs is the leader to get the state back on track.”

sources.news_title: Club for Growth PAC Congratulates Rep. Andy Biggs on AZ-GOV Primary Victory
sources.text:
Club for Growth PAC Congratulates Rep. Andy Biggs on AZ-GOV Primary Victory
Washington, D.C. – Club for Growth PAC congratulates Rep. Andy Biggs (CFGF Lifetime Rating: 99%) on winning the Republican nomination for Governor in Arizona. Biggs, a 9-time winner of the Club for Growth’s Defender of Economic Freedom Award, will face incumbent Democrat and school freedom opponent Katie Hobbs in the general election. President Donald Trump has also endorsed Biggs in the race.
“Andy Biggs is a principled conservative focused on limited government and individual freedom,” said Club for Growth PAC President David McIntosh. “Biggs is a proven winner with clear momentum in the race. He is the ideal candidate to take down Katie Hobbs and restore common sense to Phoenix.”
